title: DeepInfer: High-performance inference framework for DeepSeek models
titleZh: DeepInfer: High-performance inference framework for DeepSeek models
author: ggcr
relevanceReason: 命中 2 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: DeepInfer is the high-performance inference framework that powers DeepSeek's large-scale production services. This open-source release provides offline inference with the core features needed for serving at scale. Supported models:

Optimized kernels, model and sampler runtime Parallelism: Attention DP / balanced CP, MoE EP + EPLB DSpark and confidence-scheduled verification SWA bounded replay Asynchronous scheduling (zero-overhead batch scheduler) Batch-invariant inference Deterministic sampling Structured outputs

comments.author: schneehertz
comments.textRawHtml:
A nuclear bomb

"Based on this framework, we have achieved high-throughput, low-latency large-scale inference services for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Currently, the service throughput of a single cluster is 155 trillion tokens/day, and the overall revenue is $38 per card per hour (at off-peak pricing)"

Source: https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/2095560295930508953

children.author: abound
children.textRawHtml:
It's really refreshing to put some cold hard numbers on this stuff, hopefully this quells some of the "AI is unprofitable everyone is spending a dollar to make fifty cents" arguments. Amortized cost of owning a DC full of GPUs is far less than $38/card/hr

Not to say it can't still be a bubble, just that there is legitimately profit to be had and perhaps some sustainable equilibrium in the future.

children.author: Closi
children.textRawHtml:
> hopefully this quells some of the "AI is unprofitable everyone is spending a dollar to make fifty cents" arguments.

I think everyone has known that inference is profitable overall for the major providers for a while (I'm sure not all user accounts, but in aggregate).

The major providers are unprofitable after you add in the training and research costs and other overheads.

This is why the open source models are such a threat if they become good enough - it will destroy the business model of just providing raw chat/intelligence.

Arguably that's also why a few of these providers are trying to diversify into whole-platform approaches rather than just relying on having their whole thing be a great model.

children.author: jeremyjh
children.textRawHtml:
There has always been a lot of evidence that prices are only going down. The fact that you could already get DeepSeek or GLM inference from 20+ providers on openrouter.ai was already sufficient evidence that inference was profitable and being commoditized.

People that want to believe something different as a coping mechanism will not be swayed by this evidence either.

children.textRawHtml: Yesterday’s frontier is today’s commodity, so I don't think frontier AI is out of reach. With computing and solar energy costs continuing to drop, the current AI supply shortages are just a temporary blip. We’ll probably land right back in standard boom-and-bust cycles.

children.author: Tuna-Fish
children.textRawHtml: Either frontier AI will continue to get better steadily, until it's better than people at basically everything, and very weird things start to happen, or, it plateaus and the open weights models will eventually catch up.

children.author: pegasus
children.textRawHtml: There's a third possibility, which to me is also the most plausible.  Models will keep getting better and better within certain domains, while never catching up with humans when it comes to other type of tasks. Like that elusive quality-without-a-name some have called "taste". Or knowing what UX is most intuitive to humans. Really, anything where we have to tap into our common humanity and our human experience in order to be of help to other humans and generally to life on earth. Which is an all-important skill, since the flowering of life on the earth is (or should be) the whole point of anything we do, after all.

children.author: jacquesm
children.textRawHtml:
Those cycles have shortened considerably. Just look at the lifespan of media, integrated circuits, software, products. There have been so many big model releases just in the last three months I've lost count. We're now closer to weeks between steps.

Maybe if China stops releasing capable models the pace will slow down a little, but they have lots of incentives not to.

children.author: torginus
children.textRawHtml:
It is, because just like you mentioned, there's no exponential physics to back up growth. LLMs have to stop scaling up compute, because there's only so much resources.

But even if we think back to the previous decade or two (sans AI), most of tech has been a a red queen's race - developing and improving stuff, without any real substantial results.

Microservices and orchestration are not better than old monoliths. Electron apps are not better than native. Most programs people actually use have decades-old codebases.

Video games of today don't look substantially better or play different than ones from 15 years ago.
